text: "This awful language has escaped the browser and infiltrated our servers." That was a Hacker News commenter writing about JavaScript in 2014. You see, JavaScript has never been the most loved language, but in 2026, still it runs the world's infrastructure. So how did that happen? Let's answer the most important question first. How did JavaScript came to be? In May 1995, Netscape needed a scripting language for the browser. Java was too heavy. It required a virtual machine, a class file format, a separate runtime download. C was unthinkable and too low-level. They needed something a webpage author, a designer, a marketer, an intern could actually write. So they hired a 33-year-old engineer named Brendan Eich and gave him a deadline, 10 days. He also shipped a working prototype in 10 days. They called it Mocha. By September of 1995, it was called LiveScript. By December that same year, they renamed it to JavaScript. At this point, the language had more aliases than your bashrc file, but the name was a marketing move. This, in quote, "awful language" has nothing to do with Java. You see, Java was a cool name back then, and associating with Java meant you are also cool. Same energy as slapping AI on your startup today. You did nothing different, but suddenly you are adjacent to genius. So with time, every browser shipped with Mocha. Hey, no, LiveScript. Hey, sorry, guys, they shipped with JavaScript. JavaScript wasn't designed to win. It was designed to be available, readily available. Those two are different things. So guys, that begs the question, how the hell did JavaScript get to the server? For 14 years, it didn't. The server ran Perl, then PHP, then Python, then Ruby. JavaScript has always lived inside the browser, and most people thought it would die there. But in November 2009, that was when an engineer, Ryan Dahl, walked into a stage in Berlin in front of 150 people. He'd been watching Apache choke under con... He'd been watching Apache choke under concurrent connections. Every request opened a new thread. Every thread ate memory. The server collapsed too... The server collapsed when too many users showed up at once. He wanted something different, a server that didn't block, and he chose JavaScript. And he chose JavaScript. He was reaching for a ten-day-old language to replace a battle-tested Apache, which is to say he switched stacks about as fast as when you abandon a JS framework the second a shinier one trends on Twitter. But he chose it for a very specific reason. Every other language already had I/O built in, and it was re... and it was built around blocking. Developers who wanted async had to b-bolt it on. Developers who wanted async had to bolt it on. Ruby had EventMachine. Python had Twisted. But those libraries were fighting their own language's defaults. The second a normal blocking call slipped in, the whole thing stalled. JavaScript had no I/O library at all, no legacy, no default to fight, and JavaScript developers were the only programmers on Earth who already thought in events because that's how the browser works, and that's where they spent their whole careers. He took V8, the JavaScript engine powering Google Chrome, wrapped it in an event loop, and turned it into a server runtime. He called it Node.js. The audience gave him a standing ovation, the first in the conference's history. Within months, tens of thousands of engineers were running to it. The people who centered this for a living got to touch a database, and the database has never been the same. JavaScript had escaped the browser. And there's the line. A Hacker News commenter writing in 2014 used exactly that verb. "We allowed this awful language to escape the browser and infiltrate our servers in form of Node.js." He was writing about escape. He was right about the escape, but he didn't know what was coming next. JavaScript went to mobile and desktop. How? In 2013, an engineer at GitHub named Cheng Zhao... GitHub was building a text editor called Atom, and Atom's pitch was the hackable editor, customizable in the same language its users wrote every day, JavaScript. So Atom had to ship with a browser inside it. The runtime was called Atom Shell. Two years later, GitHub renamed it to Electron. Then in 2013, an engineer named Jordan Walke proved at an internal hackathon that React's component model could drive real native UI on iOS, not a WebView. Actual native widgets. Same JavaScript code, two mobile platforms, Android and iOS. Facebook open sourced-- Facebook open sourced it at F8 in March 2015 and called it React Native, and that was the beginning of a terror reign by JavaScript as the world's most dominant language. VS Code is Electron. Slack is Electron. Discord, Figma, Notion, 1Password, Obsidian, all Electron. Your code editor is a browser. Your password manager is a browser. Your favorite chat app is a browser too. Now, in 2024, something strange also happened. Microsoft confirmed that part of the Windows 11 start menu was built with React Native. The interface rendered into the native XAML layer underneath, not a WebView pretending to be native. Actual native UI controls described in JavaScript. And Microsoft made this choice on purpose. The recommended section pulls personalized files, recent apps, frequently changing content. It needed to ship fast and iterate fast. It needed to ship fast and iterate fast, faster than recompiling Windows could allow. So Microsoft builds and maintains its own fork, React Native for Windows, specifically so JavaScript can drive native Windows widgets. The most deployed operating system on the planet was drawing its own menu in the language one engineer wrote in ten days. In 2026, every large language model on the market appears to have been trained on code where JavaScript dominates. That means GitHub's public repos, every npm package, every blog post and answered Stack Overflow question. The most trained-on language becomes the most generated. The most generated becomes the most shipped, and the most shipped become the most-- and the most shipped become the next training corpus for the model after that. Stack Overflow 2025 survey-- Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey asked forty-nine thousand engineers what they actually use. JavaScript came in first, as it has every year for over a decade. Sixty-six percent, the single most used language on the planet. JavaScript didn't win on quality, it won on supply.
